name: Delhi's AQI
description: An interactive data visualisation that exposes how clean air in Delhi has become a privilege, using personal data and narrative to shift users from awareness to discomfort.

sections.label: The Deliberate Absence of an Exit

contentBlocks.content: A Data Visualisation on the Privilege of Clean Air

Delhi's AQI is a browser-based interactive experience, built over one week for a college exhibition, that turns something normally abstract â€” air pollution exposure â€” into something a person can hold in their hand. It asks a visitor a short series of questions about their daily routine, calculates exactly how much toxic air their income has let them avoid, and then prints out a receipt. But the receipt they walk away with is not their own. It belongs to someone else â€” someone from their daily life who has been absorbing the exposure they paid to avoid.
Delhi has one of the worst air quality crises on the planet. But its upper-middle class has largely normalised it. They've checked the AQI app, bought a purifier, and moved on.

The problem was never a lack of awareness. It's that clean air has been privatised. A sealed apartment and a HEPA filter aren't solutions â€” they're an exit, available only to people who can afford one. The air outside that apartment, the commons everyone else still has to breathe, stays exactly as toxic as it was before.

This project isn't trying to spread awareness people already have. It's trying to make something uncomfortable that money has made very easy to ignore. If someone has the means to filter their air, seal their space, or opt out of the outdoors, they've probably stopped actually feeling the crisis, even while knowing intellectually that it exists.
This is an act of advocacy, not an explainer. It doesn't try to prescribe a solution. It tries to make visible what capital has quietly made invisible.

content: Class: Upper-middle, financially independent
Location: Delhi / NCR

contentBlocks.content: This isn't the demographic most affected by the air quality crisis. It's the demographic most equipped to do something about it. They hold the economic power, the social influence, and the political voice needed to demand systemic change â€” and they are also, not coincidentally, the demographic least confronted with the need to.
An Interface People Already Trust

The interface was deliberately built to look like a premium fitness or finance dashboard â€” a visual language this specific audience already trusts and feels comfortable inside. The visitor builds their day using sliders and toggles: hours in an AC car, hours in a filtered office, hours at home with a purifier running. It creates a small, satisfying sense of control. They are, in effect, building their own "clean air bubble."
The Pivot

Once that bubble is calculated, the interface introduces a variable the visitor cannot control: a second, parallel dataset belonging to someone else entirely â€” someone from their own daily life, like the person who delivers their groceries. The discomfort isn't an accident of the visuals. It comes from realising that personal safety, in this system, is a luxury being purchased â€” and that it relies on someone else absorbing what you've paid to avoid.
Why the Second Person Has No Name

This was the single most deliberate ethical decision in the whole project, and the one most likely to get pushed back on in a crit: the second persona is not a real, named individual. It's an occupational data composite â€” built from aggregate government labour data, gig platform research, and epidemiological studies on outdoor worker exposure, not from one person's story.
In practice, that means:

content: No name
No face
No backstory
No suffering shown as spectacle

contentBlocks.content: Their timeline is never shown smaller, dimmer, or subordinate to the visitor's. It runs in parallel, equally legible, treated with the same formal dignity as the visitor's own data.
Every major creative choice on this project was locked early and held to deliberately, rather than drifting during execution:

content: Emotional mechanism â€” Dissonance, not guilt
Narrative structure â€” Three beats: Body â†’ Shield â†’ System
Opening â€” Single line of text, dark background, zero UI chrome
Persona framing â€” Occupational data composite, not a human being. No name, no face, no biography
Call to action at the end â€” None. Three structural data points (policy levers) only
Colour direction â€” Monochromatic, one meaningful accent colour, a biological shift in that accent as accumulation data appears
Typography â€” Serious publication register, not health-app register
Individual exit â€” Deliberately absent â€” structural claustrophobia is the point

contentBlocks.content: The tone was built as a deliberate synthesis of two different standards, rather than picking one. The journalism standard â€” outlets like The Pudding, Periscopic, and Reuters Graphics â€” is data that has a point of view, doesn't hide behind "we just show the numbers," and treats the reader as an adult. The design standard â€” Giorgia Lupi's hand-drawn data portraits, Nadieh Bremer's organic systems, the New York Times Climate desk's long-form scrollers â€” is work where every typographic and colour decision is a considered argument, not decoration.

The synthesis: the data has a position, and the design embodies that position without decorating it. Practically, that meant a monochromatic palette with one accent colour used sparingly; no infographic clichÃ©s; no icons of lungs with red zones; no warning symbols. The discomfort in this piece was always meant to come from clarity, not from visual alarm.
Every number the piece shows a visitor is calculated live from their own inputs, using published, citable methodology rather than an invented scoring system.
Calculation 1 â€” Weighted Daily Exposure (TWA)

A person doesn't breathe the same air all day. A purifier cleans the air at home, an office has its own HVAC, a commute happens inside an AC car â€” but outside is the full ambient concentration. This formula takes a time-weighted average across every environment someone moves through, weighted by how many hours they actually spend in each one.

contentBlocks.content: That works out to a weighted exposure of roughly 98.4 Î¼g/mÂ³ â€” more than double the upper-middle-class user, on the same day, in the same city. The reason this uses a time-weighted average rather than a single AQI reading is that a fixed outdoor sensor doesn't reflect personal exposure at all â€” someone sealed inside a filtered apartment all day has a completely different exposure than the number posted outside their window. TWA is the standard the WHO and occupational health bodies use for exactly this kind of calculation.
Calculation 2 â€” Cigarette Equivalent

PM2.5 concentration in Î¼g/mÂ³ is invisible and abstract â€” "47.7 Î¼g/mÂ³" means very little to most people on its own. Berkeley Earth found a way to make it tangible: they calculated that breathing air at a sustained 22 Î¼g/mÂ³ of PM2.5 for a full day does roughly the same lung damage as smoking one cigarette.
Cigarettes per day = Daily PM2.5 (Î¼g/mÂ³) Ã· 22

content: Upper-middle-class user (47.7 Î¼g/mÂ³): 47.7 Ã· 22 = 2.2 cigarettes/day â€” cigarettes they never chose to smoke
Gig delivery rider (98.4 Î¼g/mÂ³): 98.4 Ã· 22 = 4.5 cigarettes/day
Street vendor (126.4 Î¼g/mÂ³): 126.4 Ã· 22 = 5.7 cigarettes/day

contentBlocks.content: This is Berkeley Earth's published constant, derived from comparative toxicological studies on PM2.5 and tobacco smoke particulate damage, and it's widely used and cited in air quality research.
The Clean Air Privilege Score

This one deliberately isn't a custom formula. It's not meant to look precise for its own sake â€” because it isn't measuring an individual's uniqueness, it's placing them inside a group. Roughly 12% of Delhi's population falls into the upper-middle-class bracket this piece targets, and a visitor's privilege rank is essentially their position relative to that slice of the city, not a bespoke personal calculation. That was an intentional choice: the score is about where someone sits in a structure shared by a defined group of people, not about flattering them with a unique number.

contentBlocks.content: The results surface without any dramatisation. Just the number, a label, and a source. The weight comes from precision, not from styling.
Phase 2: The Choice
A single question appears on screen:
"Who in your daily life do you interact with the most?"

contentBlocks.caption: The one moment in the whole flow where the visitor makes a choice rather than a measurement.

contentBlocks.content: Four options, each deliberately framed as a relationship rather than a job title:

content: The person who delivers your food and groceries
The person who helps run your home
The person who guards your building
The person who sells you things on the street

contentBlocks.content: Phase 3: The Receipt
The output is a two-column receipt. The left column is headed PERSONAL AIR EXPOSURE RECEIPT. The right is headed EXPOSURE BILL â€” UNPAID. Both columns carry identical line items, side by side:

content: Daily exposure profile (commute, indoor, outdoor, weighted average) in Î¼g/mÂ³
Cigarette equivalent
Disease risk elevation, calculated differently per profile because risk scales with exposure
Privilege Rank

contentBlocks.caption: The visitor's own receipt on screen â€” precise, unstyled, and printable.
Once downloaded, the line "This person's lungs have been charged accordingly" appears â€” the only moment the piece raises its voice.

contentBlocks.content: At the bottom of each column sits a coloured box. The visitor's is dark green, explaining their protected position. The worker's is dark red, explaining what they'll pay for that protection â€” not in money, but in lung capacity and years. Below both columns, a single final line closes the piece:
"Clean air was not distributed. It was purchased."
There is no button. No call to action. No individual resolution offered. The receipt ends, and the page ends with it.

The Clean Air Privilege Score doesn't end with a number. It ends with a mirror and a map. The mirror: here is your position in this system, here is what it cost you, here is what it cost someone else. The map: here is what systemic change actually looks like, here is who has the power to demand it, here is what has and hasn't been tried.

Most data dashboards end with "here's what you can do." This one ends with "here's what you can't do alone." That gap, between seeing the problem clearly and having no individual exit from it, is where the real discomfort lives â€” and discomfort without an easy exit is what actually tends to push people toward the one thing that works: collective political pressure, not individual purchases.

The build was kept deliberately simple: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework layered on top. The visitor's inputs run directly through the exposure calculations client-side, and the output receipt is generated as a downloadable image.

The printer connection is the part people usually assume was more complicated than it was. The browser never actually talks to the thermal printer directly. During the exhibition, every downloaded receipt landed in a watched "hot folder" on the machine running the display â€” a folder set up to monitor itself for new files. The moment a new receipt image appeared there, it was automatically sent straight to the thermal printer, with no manual step in between. A visitor pressed download, and a printed receipt was already in their hand moments later, without either of them touching a print dialogue.

contentBlocks.content: This was built and shown inside a college exhibition â€” a small, in-person setting rather than a large public installation. The thermal printer sat physically on site, printing receipts as visitors went through the experience, so the final object each person left with was a real, physical piece of paper, not just something on a screen.
